paper_title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, benchmark of 3.06 million coordinatesupervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, claim-independent verifier that estimates the observations source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold. Our code and data are released at GitHub1. 1. Introduction Visual agents explore whole-slide images by requesting magnified views [5, 6, 34]. Each observation carries 1https://github.com/Yan2266336/PyraFault claimed location that connects local evidence to its reference context. An agent may correctly interpret magnified observation yet attribute it to the wrong location, turning valid visual content into misleading spatial evidence. This raises question: when does visual match provide sufficient evidence of claimed spatial origin? Figure 1 shows plausible observation from another location with similar tissue structures. Such mismatches may arise from pyramid-coordinate conversion errors or incorrect content metadata associations [11, 15]. Matching and localization [29, 30] face three challenges here. Magnification changes visual detail: 512 512 query occupies only 128 128 context pixels in our setting, where cellular details may be absent. Repeated tissue structures support competing locations, connecting provenance verification to ambiguity in visual place recognition [22, 35]. Sources may lie outside the context, elsewhere on the same slide or on another slide, even when an in-context match appears plausible. Therefore, verification must assess spatial agreement and permit abstention when evidence is insufficient. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV): given magnified query, lower-magnification context, and claimed location, evaluate the spatial claim, recover the source within the context when possible, and abstain under uncertainty. PyraFault provides 3.06 million examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts. Pyramid coordinates and slide identities establish true sources independently of claims. PyraFault includes controlled provenance faults, appearance-mined alternatives, and geometric viewing perturbations. The test set samples all eight conditions equally, with 12.5% correct claims. Our verifier, ZoomTrace, estimates the source and its reliability before consulting the claim. It aligns physical scale, retrieves candidates using frozen features, and refines locations through geometric matching. Building on matching uncertainty [22, 35], reliability compares the strongest Figure 1. Cross-magnification provenance verification in whole-slide pathology image. (a) The reference context shows the claimed location (red), ground-truth source (green), and ZoomTrace prediction (blue dashed). (b) The returned high-magnification observation originates from the true source rather than the claimed location. (c) The claimed and actual source regions exhibit visually similar tissue structures. ZoomTrace independently recovers the source (IoU = 0.998) and correctly identifies the provenance mismatch. match with spatially disjoint alternatives; overlapping windows may represent the same source. The final decision combines sourceclaim agreement with reliability, enabling verification, mismatch detection, or abstention, and local source recovery for incorrect claims. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace reaches AUPRC 0.969 and AUROC 0.987, versus 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Ablations support scale alignment, refinement, and candidate diversity. Winning-score confidence gives stronger aggregate discrimination, while disjoint competition yields more uniform coverage across perturbations. Seven VLMs show limited claim-free localization in the tested settings; CAMELYON16 exposes retrieval and calibration limitations. Verification reduces exposure and silent failures; verdict gains vary by agent and threshold. Our contributions are: (1) CMPV, task for spatial provenance discrimination, local source recovery, and selective decisions across magnifications; (2) PyraFault, coordinate-supervised benchmark of controlled provenance faults; and (3) ZoomTrace, claim-independent verifier combining geometric localization with competing-source reliability, evaluated through component studies and visualagent interventions. 2. Related Work Visual agents and evidence acquisition. V* [32] and ZoomEye [28] guide detailed image exploration. PathAgent [6], GIANT [5], and PathNavigate [34] extend navigation and evidence selection to gigapixel pathology, while PathAgentBench [18] evaluates retrieval, localization, and multi-scale reasoning. MedVIGIL studies recognition of broken visual evidence in medical question answering [16]. PathTrace audits recorded navigation and evidence traces of pathology agents [19]. Image provenance analysis reconstructs source relationships and transformation histories among related images [23]. CMPV instead verifies whether magnified observation originates from its claimed spatial location using independent visual evidence. Correspondence and uncertainty. Histopathology registration aligns tissue images across sections or staining conditions [4, 12, 31]. CMPV instead evaluates local observations claimed source, including cases where the source is absent from the reference context. LoFTR [29], Efficient LoFTR [30], LightGlue [20], and RoMa [10] establish geometric correspondences; MatchAnything [14] and MINIMA [27] extend matching across appearance changes. DINOv2 [26] and UNI [7] provide frozen retrieval representations. Relative match distinctiveness is used in Lowes ratio test [21] and place-recognition uncertainty methods, including SUE [35] and Statistical Uncertainty [22]. ZoomTrace applies related principle at the candidate-region level, comparing the strongest geometric match against spatially disjoint alternatives to estimate source reliability. Selective prediction [13] provides an accuracycoverage perspective for comparing verifiers with different answering rates. 3. Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification Inputs and supervision. We evaluate nine frozen-model verifiers on all 503,320 test pairs: ZoomTrace; Efficient LoFTR [30], SuperPoint + LightGlue [9, 20], MatchAnythingELoFTR [14], RoMa [10], and MINIMA LightGlue [27]; retrieval uncertainty methods SUE [35] and Statistical Uncertainty [22]; and NCC [17]. (6) AUPRC (average precision) and AUROC use all pairs, including abstentions, with correct claims positive. Decision coverage is the non-abstaining fraction; balanced accuracy (BA) is conditional on that subset. Localization uses median source IoU and the number of returned in-context estimates, independently of abstention. Protocols are in Supplement A. 6.1. Benchmark Performance and Provenance Failures Discrimination and source recovery. ZoomTrace combines strong claim discrimination with broad source recovery  (Table 2)  . It achieves AUPRC 0.969 and AUROC 0.987, versus 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Median source IoU is 0.799 over all 251,660 in-context examples; Efficient LoFTR reaches 0.962 on 208,334 estimates. Recovery recall instead counts missing estimates as failures on all 188,745 incorrect claims with in-context sources. At IoU 0.5, ZoomTrace recovers 97.26%, versus 82.75% for Efficient LoFTR (Supplement C.3). On 210,647 shared estimates, ZoomTrace also leads in discrimination: AUPRC 0.976 versus 0.926 and AUROC 0.987 versus 0.977 (Supplement C.2). Selective decisions. At τw, exposure falls from 1.000 to 0.538, 0.519, and 0.453  (Table 8)  ; silent failures decrease from 0.769/0.785/0.481 to 0.423/0.392/0.179, respectively. Claude Codes verdict accuracy improves from 0.521 to 0.756, with 19 corrected versus 3 newly incorrect verdicts (exact McNemar = 8.6 104). DeepSeek improves numerically from 0.755 to 0.829, with 20 corrected versus 12 newly incorrect (p = 0.22); Codex remains at 0.987. Silentfailure reductions are significant for Claude and DeepSeek (p = 3.5 106 and 2.1 105). The benchmark threshold produces smaller exposure reductions and no uniform accuracy benefit: DeepSeeks accuracy is 0.689 at τb, versus 0.755 without protection. Practical execution. The PathAgent bridge measures 2.3 for reading reference context, 5.7 for constructing its descriptor bank, and 0.5 for verification. The bank can be reused for subsequent queries within the same context. PathAgent. At τb, the PathAgent bridge [6] withholds 12/31 adjacent-drift, 0/31 within-context, and 2/31 out-ofslide observations, no clean views withheld. Provenance answers remain unchanged across arms. Its precomputed navigation features limit the downstream effects observable from substituted pixels. See Supplement H.2 for details. 7. Conclusion CMPV and PyraFault make it possible to evaluate whether visual agents can trust the spatial origins of their magnified observations. ZoomTraces independent localization supports claim discrimination and source correction; direct claim matching offers strong discrimination at lower cost. Reliability experiments reveal trade-off between winningscore discrimination and more uniform coverage from disjoint competition. Tool-path verification reduces exposure, with verdict gains depending on the agent and threshold. Retrieval under source shift and calibration sensitivity to large residuals remain the main constraints on broader use.

sections.content: OpenAI Codex assisted with improving the clarity and presentation of the manuscript draft and refining the LaTeX layout. Claude Code assisted with implementing experimental protocols and writing the corresponding evaluation code. The VLMs and agent harnesses evaluated as experimental systems are identified in Section 6 and the supplementary protocols.
